article.overview: A ground-penetrating radar (GPR) is an active geophysical instrument that transmits short pulses of radio-frequency energy into the ground and records the weak echoes returned from buried interfaces. On the Moon, a surface GPR carried by a rover can map the shallow stratigraphy of the regolith and upper crust. The best-documented flown examples in the sources reviewed are the dual-frequency Lunar Penetrating Radar (LPR) systems carried by China's Yutu (Chang'e-3) and Yutu-2 (Chang'e-4) rovers [1][2]. Radar sounders in lunar orbit, such as the SELENE (Kaguya) Lunar Radar Sounder and the Apollo 17 Lunar Sounder Experiment, use related radar principles but look down from orbit. They are included here as related instruments and are kept separate from the surface examples [3][4].
article.description:
A ground-penetrating radar transmits a short electromagnetic pulse into the ground through an antenna. A receiver then records the echoes that return from places where the electrical properties of the material change, such as boundaries between regolith layers, buried rocks or contacts between different rock units. The time between transmission and echo, together with the strength and shape of the returned signal, is used to infer where those boundaries lie. Unlike a passive seismometer, a GPR does not depend on natural events; it generates its own signal, so mapping can be scheduled by mission operators.

On the Moon, a surface GPR is normally carried on a rover or lander and operated from the lunar surface. The Chang'e-3 and Chang'e-4 LPR systems each used two frequency channels: a lower-frequency channel intended to probe deeper and a higher-frequency channel intended to resolve shallower structure [1][2]. The Chang'e-4 analysis used only the high-frequency channel, because the low-frequency data were affected by coupling with the rover body [1].

The term ground-penetrating radar is also used for orbital instruments in the wider literature. Orbital sounders look down from spacecraft altitude rather than sitting on the ground, and their antennas, power and data budgets are different. They are described in the physical specifications section as separate examples so that their values are not confused with those of surface radars [3][4].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of a lunar GPR is to determine shallow subsurface structure: the thickness of loose surface material, the depth and character of layers, and the location of buried rocks or boundaries. Such information helps scientists interpret how the surface has been built up by impacts, volcanism and the redistribution of fragments, and it provides ground truth for interpreting orbital observations. The Chang'e-4 study used its radar data to interpret shallow layering on the lunar farside. It divided the shallow subsurface into units at roughly 0-12 m, 12-24 m and 24-40 m, and stated that the upper contact of a basal mare layer must be deeper than 40 m [1]. Engineering applications include estimating regolith thickness, which is relevant to excavation, drilling and sampling planning. The sources reviewed for this article do not assess such engineering use cases in detail, so these applications are stated as conceptual.
article.operating_principle: A GPR radiates a short pulse or chirp through its antenna into the surface. As the wave moves into the ground it travels at a speed that depends on the dielectric permittivity of the material. Part of the wave is reflected wherever permittivity changes, and the remainder continues deeper. The receiver records the echo as a function of two-way travel time. For an assumed wave velocity v and two-way travel time t, the approximate depth of a reflector is d = v x t / 2. The Chang'e-4 study used a wave velocity of 0.16 m/ns for this depth conversion [1]. Depths derived this way therefore carry the uncertainty of the velocity assumption. Frequency sets the trade-off between penetration and resolution: higher frequencies resolve finer features but attenuate more quickly, while lower frequencies penetrate further but resolve less detail. Processing such as migration or tomographic inversion is used to focus reflections into interpretable images [1]. The depth actually reached depends on local electrical properties, which the sources reviewed here do not describe for the whole regolith. Penetration depths are therefore reported only for specific sites and processing assumptions [1][2].
article.scientific_importance: Ground-penetrating radar gives direct information about shallow subsurface structure that surface images cannot provide. The Chang'e-4 LPR study reported shallow layering on the lunar farside, interpreted from radar reflections that the authors related to surface and near-surface units [1]. These results matter for understanding how the farside surface has evolved and for interpreting the geology recorded in orbital data. The Chang'e-3 record is more contested. A 2022 study compared the lunar data with a prototype radar mounted on a model of the rover and concluded that some deep features previously attributed to shallow lunar stratigraphy are likely artefacts from the radar system and its electromagnetic interaction with the metallic rover [2]. The scientific value of a lunar GPR therefore depends on careful calibration, analysis of rover coupling, and comparison of results with independent measurements.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a ground-penetrating radar. Surface and orbital radars differ in frequency, antenna geometry, power, mounting and data systems. The examples below describe specific flown instruments. Where a value is not supported by the sources reviewed, it is recorded as not publicly specified. Surface and orbital examples are not directly comparable.

examples.name: Chang'e-3 Lunar Penetrating Radar (CE-3 LPR)

frequency_channels.antenna: Pair of monopoles, about 1.15 m long, separated by about 0.8 m, suspended about 0.6 m above the ground at the back of the rover
One transmitter and two receiver bowtie antennas on the rover underside, about 0.3 m above the ground, 0.16 m between receivers

examples.dimensions: Complete LPR unit dimensions not publicly specified in the sources reviewed; antenna dimensions given above.
examples.qualification: The 40-80 MHz and 250-750 MHz band limits and antenna geometry come from the Chang'e-4 paper [1], which describes the design as the same as CE-3. The 60 MHz and 500 MHz working frequencies come from the CE-3 analysis [2]. The primary 2014 CE-3 LPR instrument paper was not accessed.
examples.narrative: The Chang'e-3 LPR flew on the Yutu rover, which separated from the Chang'e-3 lander on 14 December 2013 [2]. The system has two frequency channels. The lower-frequency channel has a 60 MHz centre frequency and a 40-80 MHz band. It uses a pair of monopole antennas, each about 1.15 m long, separated by about 0.8 m and suspended about 0.6 m above the ground at the back of the rover [1]. The higher-frequency channel has a 500 MHz centre frequency and a 250-750 MHz band. It uses one transmitting and two receiving bowtie antennas on the underside of the rover, about 0.3 m above the ground with 0.16 m between the receivers [1]. The working frequencies of 60 MHz and 500 MHz for the two radar systems are stated in [2]. The band limits and antenna geometry are stated in [1] for the same dual-frequency design, which the Chang'e-4 paper describes as the CE-3 design. Mass, power and complete unit dimensions were not found in the sources reviewed. The rover covered about 114 m during roughly two weeks of data collection, and it became stuck at navigation point N0209, after which data were collected only from a fixed position [2].

examples.name: Chang'e-4 Lunar Penetrating Radar (Yutu-2)
examples.platform: Yutu-2 rover, which landed with the Chang'e-4 lander at Von Karman crater

frequency_channels.antenna: One transmitter and two receivers (CH2A, CH2B) at the rover bottom, about 0.3 m above the ground; CH2B used for analysis
Pair of monopoles at the rover back, about 1.15 m long, 0.8 m apart, 0.6 m above the ground

examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed; antenna dimensions given above.
examples.qualification: Values are as stated in the Chang'e-4 paper [1]. The paper gives no formal vertical or horizontal resolution figure; it states that scatterers larger than about half the signal wavelength (about 0.2 m) can be resolved by the tomographic method.
examples.narrative: The Chang'e-4 LPR flew on the Yutu-2 rover, which landed with the Chang'e-4 lander at Von Karman crater. The paper describes the rover as equipped with the same dual-frequency Lunar Penetrating Radar used on Chang'e-3 [1]. The published analysis used only the high-frequency channel, specifically the receiver CH2B, because CH2A showed strong cross-talk. The low-frequency data were excluded because of coupling with the rover body [1]. The paper reports that a signal was detected to about 500 ns two-way travel time, which it describes as over three times the Chang'e-3 penetration of about 150 ns [1]. Mass, power and dimensions were not reported in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: SELENE (Kaguya) Lunar Radar Sounder (LRS)
examples.type: Flown lunar orbital radar sounder (related instrument, not a surface GPR)

frequency_channels.antenna: Two sets of 30 m tip-to-tip long dipoles

examples.dimensions: Not stated on the JAXA page; antenna length given above.
examples.qualification: Values are JAXA-stated mission specifications from a single page [3]. The 5 km sounding depth is a JAXA-stated value and was not independently checked. The instrument paper (Ono et al., 2010, Space Science Reviews) was not accessed.
examples.narrative: The SELENE (Kaguya) Lunar Radar Sounder was an orbital instrument. JAXA's equipment page gives a mass of 23.182 kg and power of 56.7 W, a main radar frequency of 5 MHz, a radiated power of 800 W, a pulse width of 200 microseconds and a modulation of 10 kHz per microsecond. JAXA also states a sounding depth of 5 km and a range resolution of less than 100 m [3]. The radar used two sets of 30 m tip-to-tip long dipole antennas for the 5 MHz observation [3]. The same instrument also received natural plasma waves and planetary radio emissions over 10 Hz to 30 MHz [3]. The mass and power figures come from a single JAXA source and were not cross-checked against the instrument paper. The diagram below shows the observation principle; the test-setup photograph shows the ground test configuration [3].

examples.dimensions: Overall dimensions and dipole length not stated in the sources reviewed.
examples.qualification: Frequency and bandwidth values are from a secondary summary citing Porcello et al. (1974), which was not accessed. The 43 kg and 103 W statements are uncited on the summary page. A conflicting total-power figure exists in another secondary summary, so power is not treated as verified. Mission frequencies are given as 5, 15 and 150 MHz in the same source.
examples.narrative: The Apollo 17 Lunar Sounder Experiment (ALSE) flew on Apollo 17 in December 1972 as an orbital radar sounder [4]. A secondary summary of its design, which cites Porcello et al. (1974), gives channel frequencies of 5.266 MHz (HF1), 15.8 MHz (HF2) and 158 MHz (VHF), with chirp bandwidths of 0.5333 MHz, 1.6 MHz and 16.0 MHz [4]. The same article also describes the mission frequencies as 5, 15 and 150 MHz [4]. These values differ in rounding and should be checked against the original 1974 paper, which was not accessed. The two HF channels shared a centre-fed dipole whose two halves were retractable on opposite sides of the service module. The VHF channel used a 7-element Yagi antenna that was stowed and deployed after launch [4]. The article states that the whole system weighed 43 kg and required 103 W, but that sentence has no inline citation, and a conflicting total-power figure appears in a separate secondary summary. The power value is therefore not treated as verified. The image below is an ALSE data image of the Aitken Basin region, with its source page given in the caption [4][5].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Surface GPR antennas in the sources reviewed are small relative to the rover: the low-frequency monopoles are about 1.15 m long with 0.8 m separation, and the high-frequency bowties sit about 0.3 m above the ground with 0.16 m between receivers [1]. The complete LPR unit dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The orbital sounders use much larger antennas: the Kaguya dipoles are 30 m tip to tip [3], and the ALSE overall antenna length is not stated in the sources reviewed [4].
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Kaguya LRS: 23.182 kg, a single JAXA-stated value [3]. ALSE: 43 kg, from a secondary summary without an inline citation [4]. Chang'e-3 and Chang'e-4 LPR: not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. Mass figures for different instruments should not be compared directly, because they describe different architectures and mission roles.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Kaguya LRS: 56.7 W, with a radiated power of 800 W, both JAXA-stated [3]. ALSE: 103 W in one secondary summary, with a conflicting figure in another; not verified [4]. Chang'e-3 and Chang'e-4 LPR: not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A surface GPR on the Moon must operate through the same vacuum, thermal cycling, radiation and dust as other surface instruments, and its electrical performance must remain stable as its surroundings change. The sources show that antenna height and rover coupling strongly affect the measurements. The Chang'e-4 analysis excluded low-frequency data because of coupling with the rover body [1], and the Chang'e-3 reinterpretation attributes some deep returns to electromagnetic interaction with the metallic rover [2]. Antenna height, orientation and the electrical environment of the vehicle are therefore operational design constraints. Orbital sounders face different constraints, such as large deployable antennas and orbit geometry [3][4]. Qualification levels and environmental test results for these instruments were not found in the sources reviewed, and none are stated here.
article.limitations: A surface GPR produces a profile along its traverse rather than a map. The Chang'e-3 rover covered about 114 m during roughly two weeks of data collection [2], so its dataset is a line of radar profiles, not a survey of an area. Lower frequencies probe deeper but resolve less, and higher frequencies resolve finer detail but penetrate less [1]. Depth values depend on the wave velocity assumed in processing [1]. Rover-body interference is significant. The Chang'e-4 team excluded its low-frequency channel for this reason [1], and the Chang'e-3 deep-reflector interpretation is contested [2]. Orbital sounders cover much larger areas but at coarser surface resolution; JAXA states a range resolution of less than 100 m for the Kaguya LRS [3].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A surface GPR is normally delivered as part of a rover or lander payload. The Chang'e-3 and Chang'e-4 radars were carried on rovers that were delivered by their landers; the Chang'e-3 rover separated from its lander on 14 December 2013 [2]. The antennas are mounted on the rover body, with monopoles at the back and bowtie antennas underneath [1]. An orbital sounder is delivered as a spacecraft instrument, and its antennas are deployed after launch. The ALSE VHF Yagi was stowed and deployed after launch and the HF dipole halves were retractable [4]. The Kaguya LRS used two sets of 30 m dipoles [3].
transportation_process: Integrate the radar transmitter, receiver and antennas with the rover or spacecraft on Earth, with antennas mounted at their specified heights and orientations [1].
Launch the lander and rover, or the spacecraft, on a launch vehicle and transfer them toward the Moon.
Land the lander and separate the rover; the Chang'e-3 rover separated on 14 December 2013 [2].
Deploy the rover from the lander and begin radar operations. For the Chang'e-3 and Chang'e-4 radars, the antenna geometry is fixed once mounted [1][2].
Connect power and data interfaces through the rover. The power and data interface details are not specified in the sources reviewed.
For orbital sounders, deploy antennas after launch, commission the instrument, and operate it in orbit [3][4].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Surface radars are mounted on the rover body with fixed antenna geometry [1]. Orbital sounders used deployable dipole antennas: the ALSE HF dipole halves were retractable and its VHF Yagi was deployed after launch [4], and the Kaguya LRS used two 30 m tip-to-tip dipole sets [3]. The deployment mechanisms themselves are not described in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Chang'e-3 (Yutu) and Chang'e-4 (Yutu-2) LPR systems are surface examples [1][2]. The Apollo 17 ALSE and the SELENE (Kaguya) LRS are orbital examples [3][4].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a specific lander or rover is asserted. The sources reviewed document rover-mounted radar operation on the Chang'e rovers, but they do not provide interface data that would allow a new GPR to be matched to a lander's mass, volume, mounting, power or data budget. Any future assessment should use verified interface documents.

article.historical_significance: The Chang'e-3 LPR operated on the Yutu rover after the rover separated from its lander in December 2013 [2]. Its data were later used both to suggest shallow stratigraphy and, after reanalysis, to show that some deep reflections may be artefacts of the radar system and rover [2]. The Chang'e-4 LPR on Yutu-2 extended surface radar investigations to the lunar farside and reported shallow subsurface layering [1]. Among orbital sounders, the Apollo 17 ALSE and the SELENE (Kaguya) LRS demonstrated radar sounding from lunar orbit [3][4]. Secondary sources report ALSE results on mare layering and wrinkle ridges [4].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Not all values were verified from primary publications. The 2014 Chang'e-3 LPR instrument paper could not be accessed, and the Chang'e-3 bandwidths and antenna values rely on the Chang'e-4 paper's description of the same design [1][2]. Mass, power and complete dimensions for the Chang'e LPR units are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The ALSE values come from a secondary summary that cites Porcello et al. (1974), which was not accessed. The NASA and Lunar and Planetary Institute pages returned HTTP 403 during research, and the USGS publication page also returned HTTP 403. The ALSE power value conflicts between two secondary sources [4]. The Kaguya LRS mass and power come from a single JAXA page; the Ono et al. (2010) instrument paper was not accessed [3]. The Chang'e-3 deep-reflector interpretation is contested [2]. The depth values reported by the Chang'e-4 team depend on a wave velocity assumption [1]. Press reports describing the Chang'e radar as the first direct measurement of lunar soil structure were not verified and are not repeated as fact. Image rights are not verified: the ALSE image is hosted on Wikimedia Commons and its original provenance was not confirmed, and JAXA reuse terms were not checked [3][5]. No surface GPR image from a verified official source was obtained, so the Chang'e examples have no images.

data_quality_notes: Catalogue match: ID 081, name 'Ground-penetrating radar', category 4 'Subsurface exploration and drilling' confirmed in lunar_payloads_catalogue_320.md.

The Chang'e-3 LPR primary instrument paper (2014) and the Chang'e-4 A&A paper were not accessed (HTTP 403 and an access check page). CE-3 band limits and antenna geometry are taken from the Chang'e-4 Science Advances paper [1], which describes the same design.
LPR mass, power and complete unit dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed and are recorded as null.

ALSE frequencies, bandwidths, antennas and the 43 kg mass come from a secondary summary citing Porcello et al. (1974), which was not accessed. The 43 kg and 103 W statements are uncited on that page. A conflicting power figure (236 W total) was reported in another secondary summary. Power is not verified.
ALSE mission frequencies (5, 15, 150 MHz) and design frequencies (5.266, 15.8, 158 MHz) differ in rounding in the same secondary source; the design values are recorded.

Kaguya LRS mass (23.182 kg), power (56.7 W), 5 MHz frequency, 800 W radiated power, 5 km sounding depth and less than 100 m range resolution are JAXA-stated values from one page. The Ono et al. (2010) instrument paper was not accessed.
The Chang'e-3 interpretation of deep reflectors is contested by a 2022 study [2]. Deep-layer claims from Chang'e-3 are therefore not presented as settled.
The Chang'e-3 traverse of about 114 m is taken from the arXiv abstract [2]. A Wikipedia infobox citation for the same figure points to a Chang'e-4 article and was not used.
Press reports describing the Chang'e radar as the first direct measurement of lunar soil structure to 30 m depth were not verified and are not repeated as fact.

Images: the JAXA diagram and test photograph were retrieved (HTTP 200) from the official JAXA LRS page's asset directory and inspected. The JAXA page text itself was read through a page summary, so the JAXA caption wording should be rechecked against the live page. The ALSE image was retrieved from Wikimedia Commons (HTTP 200); its provenance and reuse rights are not verified. No official NASA ALSE image was obtained because the NASA and LPI pages returned HTTP 403.
